rationale: A wins because it keeps the story honest under pressure: "Whoop puts a cleared ECG and an uncleared blood-pressure estimate on the same wrist" is a real regulatory angle, and "What Whoop's cardiologists actually signed off on" correctly demands numbers before anyone gets cute. B is useful, but it overreaches with "bets the next fight is blood pressure" and "cuffless blood pressure is the next wearable battleground" — both may be true, but the update does not prove the market has moved there. A behaves like a strategist; B occasionally behaves like a launch-day columnist looking for lift.
gaps_in_A: "Whoop finally ships the ECG its rivals already have" leans on feature-parity strategy without naming rivals; it correctly asks for names and dates, but the headline's "finally" still assumes a lateness narrative stronger than the fact block alone supports.

"What Whoop's cardiologists actually signed off on" is strong, but calling the story type "data" is a little generous until validation metrics exist; the set does flag that the angle dies without numbers.
The valuation appears in the competitor angle — "privately held company last valued at $3.6B" — but A does not fully explain why that valuation materially changes the wearables parity story.
gaps_in_B: "catch-up-and-leapfrog story" is decorated beyond the facts. Competitors already ship ECG, but nothing supplied proves Whoop leapfrogs anyone with a non-medical BP estimate.
"the average wearer can't tell the difference" is invented user behavior. Plausible, yes; grounded, no. A reporter can investigate that, but the angle set cannot assert it from this update.
"Cuffless blood pressure is the next wearable battleground" turns one Whoop launch into a category thesis without outside evidence. That is a trend claim wearing borrowed shoes.
"Privately held at $3.6B, Whoop's monetization choices are the story here" is plausible but underproved; valuation alone does not make tier-gating a business-model trend.
